subject_entity.notes: North African confessor during the Decian persecution c. 250; endured prolonged imprisonment and torture; his grandmother, uncle, and another uncle had earlier been martyred; Cyprian later appointed him as reader in the Carthaginian church; exemplar of the confessor phenomenon that complicated the lapsed controversy.

object_entity.notes: Empire-wide persecution under Emperor Decius c. 250–251; required all citizens to sacrifice to Roman gods and obtain a certificate (libellus); many Christians lapsed; triggered the controversy over readmission of the lapsed that led to the Novatian schism.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Eusebius HE 6.43 preserves Cornelius's letter explicitly naming Celerinus as confessor.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius preserves a letter of Cornelius of Rome describing Novatian's ordination irregularity: three simple and rustic bishops from Italy were brought to Rome and compelled to lay hands on Novatian by a counterfeit and vain laying on of hands; Novatian seized the bishopric by craft and treachery. Cornelius also lists the Roman clergy: forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers. More than fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons are supported by the Lord's grace and kindness.
passage.notes: Cornelius on Novatian's irregular ordination; Roman church size and clerical orders c. 251

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: But to those who have stood firm and have not been overthrown, what great joy! To those who have lapsed, medicine is not to be denied; but the lapsed must not assume that peace can be given them hastily by anyone. Let them knock at the door of the Church, but not with violence to break it down; let them beg but not presumptuously demand. Proper penance under the bishop's authority must precede reconciliation.
passage.notes: Graded penance under episcopal authority; against hasty reconciliation by confessors

object_entity.notes: First ecumenical council convened by Emperor Constantine at Nicaea in Bithynia, May–August 325 CE. Addressed the Arian controversy; produced the original Nicene Creed affirming the Son as homoousios (same substance) with the Father; condemned Arius; standardized Easter dating; addressed the Meletian schism in Egypt. Attended by ~300 bishops, mostly from the East. Jacob of Nisibis and Eusebius of Caesarea were among the attendees.

subject_entity.notes: Roman emperor 306-337 CE; first emperor to convert to Christianity. Key acts: victory at Milvian Bridge (312); co-issued Edict of Milan (313); convened First Council of Nicaea (325); moved capital to Constantinople (330). Baptized on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia (337).

object_entity.notes: Battle fought 28 October 312 CE at the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber near Rome. Constantine defeated Maxentius; associated with Constantine's vision/dream and adoption of the Chi-Rho symbol. Sources: Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 44 (dream); Eusebius Vita Constantini 1.28-29 (waking vision).

evidence.notes: Constantine led his forces to victory at Milvian Bridge 312 CE; Lactantius De Mort. Pers. 44 is the primary source.

passage.excerpt: Constantine was directed in a dream to inscribe the heavenly sign of God on the shields of his soldiers before battle.
passage.notes: De Mort. Pers. 44; earliest account of Constantine's pre-battle vision (dream version).

source.notes: Lactantius's account of the deaths of the persecutors of Christians; c. 313-315 CE. Contains primary accounts of Constantine's vision/dream and the Edict of Milan.
